There you go. PM Modi did not name Starlink specifically, but this is exactly the principle at the heart of this debate.

Telecom is no longer just “internet”. It is critical national infrastructure.

With Starlink, India has to know:

1. Can Indian agencies lawfully intercept communications when required?

2. Can every terminal be identified and geographically located?

3. Can an unregistered or smuggled terminal be automatically denied service?

4. Can India shut service in a sensitive border area during terrorism, war or national emergency?

5. Will Indian domestic traffic remain routed through Indian gateways?

6. Will operational control and monitoring facilities remain inside India?

7. Can satellite-to-satellite routing bypass Indian monitoring?

These are not imaginary concerns. India’s satellite rules explicitly require lawful interception, geographic monitoring, terminal registration, Indian gateways, domestic traffic staying within India and the ability to deny service in restricted areas. 

And India has NOT “blocked Starlink”.

- Starlink already received its GMPCS licence in June 2025.

- IN-SPACe authorised its constellation in July 2025.

- It received provisional spectrum for trials.

- India even chose administrative allocation of satellite spectrum, the approach Starlink wanted rather than the auction model Jio had pushed for.

- Jio and Airtel have both signed partnerships with Starlink.

- Starlink itself says it has now built 20 Indian gateway sites with hundreds of antennas, India-specific security controls and systems to keep Indian user data within India. 

And today the Government clarified something very important:

- Starlink, Jio Satellite and Eutelsat OneWeb are ALL undergoing security assessment and are broadly at the same regulatory stage.

So where exactly is the evidence for this “oligarchs are blocking us” story? 

Security concerns are also not theoretical.

- A Starlink terminal recovered in Manipur was later found to be non-operational there, but it has been tried and there is potential to be used again India and compromise national security.

- In Andaman case, smugglers travelling from Myanmar used a Starlink terminal during a journey involving more than 6,000 kg of methamphetamine. Indian authorities then had to demand purchaser, registration and usage-location information from Starlink.

THAT is exactly why terminal traceability matters. 

And please stop presenting India as some digitally deprived country waiting for Starlink to rescue it.

- 98.09% of Indian villages already have internet access.

- 6,31,834 villages already have 4G coverage.

- India already had more than 1.01 BILLION internet subscribers by September 2025.

Starlink can be extremely valuable for the remaining difficult 1.9% — mountains, islands, border regions, disaster zones and other dead spots.

And Starlink is not some magic 1-1.5 Gbps consumer connection either.

Starlink currently lists Residential Lite around 80-200 Mbps and normal Residential at up to 400+ Mbps depending on market and conditions. Even its Performance Gen 3 terminal lists peak throughput around 475 Mbps. Starlink itself describes gigabit capability as a network upgrade it is working toward. 

So yes Elon...

Bring Starlink to India.

Connect the last mile.

Compete with Jio, Airtel and everyone else.

India should welcome that.

But calling legitimate sovereign security scrutiny a “crime against Indians” and blaming unnamed “oligarchs” without producing evidence is not a substitute for completing the approval process.

India is not rejecting technology.

India is asking a foreign-controlled satellite network to operate under Indian security rules on Indian soil.

That what Starlink has done for country like Israel where Nations security is utmost important. 

That is not protectionism.

That is sovereignty.

Okay so this is basically US suspending the green card processing for TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, Cognizant, Capgemini and Microsoft, Adobe.

So what?

The bad?

- Remittance. India leads the world with ~$125B in annual remittances coming into thr country. The US is ~25% ($30B+). This suspension eventually means lesser high-earning Indians in the US. 

- Fewer Indians across the top jobs in the US also probably means less soft power and reduced angel capital into domestic startups.

The good? 

- If US companies can’t bring talent to the US, they probably will bring the work to India. I expect Global Capability Centers (GCCs) to further expand. India already hosts 2,100+ GCCs employing 2.4M people.

- Top engineering talent stays back to build domestic companies and AI startups here rather than working on visa uncertainty.

What else am I missing?

text:
Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. Even today, if they have to prove their loyalty to the country and the public, it is highly shameful.”

text:
Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

text:
let the bullies and abusers be bullies and abusers. when you actually go on the ground and talk to people, you realise that sometimes it only takes empathy to connect with people. it takes empathy for people to trust you, to keep a hand on your shoulder, and believe that you are genuinely trying to amplify their voice and their cause.

because no matter what we say, people are actively facing oppression, state repression, structural and policy issues right now. for example, i met Sahil's parents. they are sitting there on hunger strike. it has been five days, and what has happened? hardly any common people are coming. the media is doing its own propaganda. one politician after another comes, gives their bite, and leaves. but these parents are looking for genuine people who will genuinely support their cause. when we spoke to their advocate, they told us that none of the media organisations are even properly putting forward what the demands of the parents are, which is simply to arrest Professor Doola and the director of IIT Bombay.

then we spoke to healthcare workers, the corona warriors, basically nurses. around 1,200 people, and around 1,100 of them are women. these people are getting paid ₹14,000 a month. ₹14,000. my injection alone costs me ₹22,000 a month. imagine having to survive on ₹14,000 while doing this kind of work. these women told us that they don't even get maternal leave. pregnant women have to come and do this much labour. they don't get paternal leave either. while they are pregnant, they have to keep working; then they give birth and immediately have to keep working because otherwise they will have no money.

these are the people who worked their asses off during corona. we all saw the chaos. we all saw the absolute horror of how the government handled COVID. and these are the people who kept the system running. these are the people who keep this country running. as one comrade always tells me: if you do not treat my existential survival as existential survival for you as well, then you are not a comrade of mine.

and then we spoke to Junaid Ansari, someone who was inspired by Khalid Saifi and Sharjeel Imam. during the Shaheen Bagh movement, he got inspired by Sharjeel Imam and everybody else who was involved. he was in Mumbai and tried to do something similar here. ever since then, there has been no case against him, but the police harass him every single day. every single day he has to go and put his hazri at the police station. he was jokingly telling us that he even takes his tiffin there now. six years of this. and a day spent at the police station is a day of lost income. it is a day where he could have been working, earning money, doing something for himself, living his life. these are the real struggles people are living with right now. and they need voices.

then there is Mankhurd. there is a huge working-class population in Mankhurd. we have worked with people there in other capacities before. whenever people protest for even their basic rights, the police goes to the owners and start asking questions and harassing them. the owners, out of fear, remove the tenants. one working-class person told us that in one year alone, he had to change his house five times. five times in one year, because they keep getting harassed. so who is going to talk about all of this?

we keep talking about the larger revolution. we keep talking about working towards a revolution. i understand the systemic and structural problem. i understand capitalism. i understand the problem of Hindutva that is driving so many of these things. but what do we do about the issues at hand? what do we do about people who are struggling right now and need help right now?

i don't believe in democracy or any of these existing systems. i have my own larger politics and larger goal. but a woman who is pregnant and being forced to work because she will otherwise lose her ₹14,000 salary needs her maternal leave now. a worker needs his wages now. a family sitting on hunger strike needs their demand to be heard now. a person being forced to spend every single day at a police station needs that harassment to stop now. someone who has had to change their house five times in one year needs immediate relief now. these are not abstract political questions for these people. this is their existence.

and this is where i have reached in my own politics. people can call us revisionists. they can call us whatever they want. but i believe the communist parties in India have failed. and i believe the critiques have also failed to create enough spaces and organisations for people to join, organise, express themselves, and fight outside of the bourgeois revisionist parties that have electoral ambitions.

if i don't like any of the communist parties in india, which i don't, and if my politics does not align with any of them, that doesn't mean i stop supporting people whose immediate struggles i believe in. if AISA asks me to make a video here and there, amplify something, or join them at a protest for a cause i am also fighting for, i am going to do that for now. maybe tomorrow i will feel differently. maybe i will get tired. but today, this is how i feel. my politics should have the scope to evolve without being criminalised.

and i am very clear that i will not join any of these organisations ever, even though both of us have received offers and all of that. my larger goal and my larger politics do not align with electorally motivated parties. but i absolutely believe there is a scope for doing both: working towards the larger goal of socialism and communism, while also working on the issues immediately affecting people and trying to get them immediate relief.

because people cannot eat ideology. people cannot survive on theoretical purity. people are living through things right now.

and i am also a person who is constantly learning and evolving. i don't set myself in stone. i don't believe that i know everything. there are people far more well-read than me, people who understand politics better than me, people who understand Marxism better than me. but there has never been a doubt in my mind about my integrity or my intent to help people.

people can call us grifters. people can call us scammers. people can say whatever they want. but the fact of the matter is that we have always tried to work for people. and somehow, getting a number of followers means that suddenly you are an influencer, suddenly you are a public figure, suddenly people think they know everything about your life.

yes, having followers has given us social capital. i will never deny that. but our financial situation is horrible. people can say whatever they want about us living in Mumbai, about this and that, but they don't know anything about our lives. they don't know anything about our backgrounds. they don't know anything about the health conditions we deal with. they don't know anything about our familial trauma. they don't know anything. it is very easy to sit behind a screen and start abusing somebody.

i am honestly almost completely indifferent and desensitised to right-wingers abusing us left, right, and centre every single day. that doesn't affect me anymore. but i am still not there when it comes to people calling us grifters and scammers and questioning our integrity. that still affects me. maybe it will take some time. maybe i will reach a point where it doesn't.

and the same goes for people constantly questioning the integrity of our politics, calling us revisionists, calling us this or that, deciding what our politics is supposed to look like. but this is where i am right now. i am learning. i am evolving. i am trying to understand. and while i work towards the larger political questions i believe in, i refuse to stop seeing the people standing in front of me and the problems they are facing today.

because if we cannot stand with people in their immediate struggles, then all our talk about revolution, socialism, communism, liberation, and changing society means absolutely nothing to the person standing in front of us asking for help.

let the bullies and abusers be bullies and abusers. i would rather keep talking to people on the ground. i would rather keep listening to them. i would rather keep trying to amplify their voices. because at the end of the day, these are the people we are supposed to be fighting for.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Deepak had been residing at the newly constructed Guru Kripa Kunj Ashram in Vrindavan.

text:
NDA Petitions Karnataka Governor, Alleges Congress Is Misusing Police to Stall Voter Revision Process

​Bengaluru

Leaders of the National Democratic Alliance (#NDA) in Karnataka, comprising the Bharatiya Janata Party (#BJP) and Janata Dal Secular(#JDS), on Tuesday submitted a formal memorandum to #Governor Thaawarchand Gehlot, alleging unlawful interference by the ruling Congress government in the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (#SIR) of electoral rolls.  

​The delegation, led by Union Ministers H.D. Kumaraswamy, alongside Leaders of the Opposition R. Ashoka (Assembly) and Chalavadi Narayanaswamy (Council), accused the state government of weaponising the police apparatus against opposition party workers filing statutory objections to voter lists.  

​According to the memorandum, the SIR process is currently at the stage of notice hearings and the disposal of claims and objections. The alliance asserted that submitting objections against the inclusion of ineligible names via #Form7 is a legitimate statutory right under Rule 13(2) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and backed by #ElectionCommission of India (ECI) guidelines permitting bulk submissions by Booth Level Agents (#BLAs).

text:
RAHUL GANDHI REMOVED FROM AKASHVANI BHAVAN: A PROTEST THAT COULD NOT BE ENDED BY BARRICADES

What happened at Akashvani Bhavan on 6 October deserves to be examined beyond the political slogans.

After opposition MPs were stopped from marching towards the Election Commission, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and other leaders staged a sit-in inside the Akashvani Bhavan premises. The protest continued for nearly nine hours before Delhi Police moved in and detained them. 

The source video records Rahul Gandhi repeatedly asking the police a remarkably simple question:

“Tell me where I can sit. If there is another place where I can peacefully protest, I will go there.” 

That is the question that should concern every democracy.

If a protest is creating a genuine public inconvenience, authorities have the legitimate responsibility to regulate it. But regulation should also provide a clear, lawful and practical alternative for peaceful assembly.

Rahul Gandhi and the Opposition said they wanted to reach the Election Commission to meet the commissioners and raise their objections concerning SIR and electoral rolls. The Election Commission, however, subsequently said that it had received no formal meeting request from any political party—an important point that must also be addressed honestly. 

So there are questions for both sides:

To the protesters: Was a formal request for a meeting actually submitted, and were lawful protest conditions followed?

To the authorities: If the march could not proceed, where exactly were the elected representatives permitted to conduct their peaceful protest?

To the Election Commission: Why not create a transparent channel for elected representatives to present their documented concerns and receive an institutional response?

The allegations of “vote theft” and electoral manipulation remain political allegations and must be established through evidence and constitutional process. But the underlying questions about voter rolls, SIR and electoral transparency deserve answers—not dismissal.

Today, the confrontation has moved beyond one march.

The real test is whether India's democratic institutions can absorb dissent without treating dissent itself as the problem.

Barricades can stop a march.
Detention can end a sit-in.
Neither can substitute for an answer.

Democracy ultimately demands something stronger than silence: credible institutions, transparent processes and the freedom to question power peacefully.

text:
OPPOSITION MUST STAND FOR EVERY CITIZEN’S RIGHT TO PEACEFUL PROTEST

The appeal in this video makes a practical institutional point: when students, citizens’ collectives or activists protest, elected representatives should not remain distant. The speaker specifically suggests that INDIA-bloc MPs should be physically present at protest sites, identify the responsible senior police officer and seek clarity about the orders being given. 

That idea can be reframed around a broader democratic principle:

THE OPPOSITION’S RESPONSIBILITY IS NOT ONLY TO REPRESENT PEOPLE WHO AGREE WITH IT. IT IS TO DEFEND THE DEMOCRATIC SPACE IN WHICH EVERY CITIZEN—INCLUDING THOSE WHO DISAGREE WITH THE OPPOSITION—CAN SPEAK, ASSEMBLE AND PROTEST PEACEFULLY.

When citizens come onto the streets with legitimate grievances, MPs should be present as public representatives and constitutional witnesses.

They should:

• meet protesters and document their grievances;
• identify the senior police officer responsible for the operation;
• ask what legal order authorises restrictions or detention;
• insist that peaceful protesters are treated lawfully and humanely;
• help detainees obtain legal assistance and information about their rights;
• document allegations of excessive force and demand an impartial investigation;
• publicly distinguish peaceful protest from any genuine violence or unlawful conduct.

This is not about giving protesters immunity from the law. It is about ensuring that the law is applied transparently, proportionately and equally.

India’s Constitution protects freedom of speech and peaceful assembly, subject to reasonable restrictions. 

Recent Delhi protests have demonstrated why independent scrutiny matters: a court granting bail to 17 protesters noted allegations of assault at a police station and directed preservation of CCTV footage, while police maintained that protesters had violated restrictions and committed offences. 

Therefore, let MPs become a constitutional bridge between citizens and the state—not merely spectators when confrontation occurs.

If the police acted lawfully, let the evidence establish it.
If excessive force was used, let the evidence establish that too.
If protesters violated lawful restrictions, let due process determine responsibility.

THE ANSWER TO POLITICAL POLARISATION IS NOT MORE POLARISATION. IT IS EQUAL PROTECTION OF THE RIGHT TO QUESTION POWER.

The video’s strongest message is therefore worth putting in institutional terms:

WHEN CITIZENS PROTEST, THEIR REPRESENTATIVES SHOULD SHOW UP.
WHEN POWER ACTS, SOMEONE SHOULD WATCH.
WHEN RIGHTS ARE QUESTIONED, THE LAW MUST SPEAK.

That standard should apply regardless of ideology, party affiliation or the identity of the protesters.

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

quotedTweet.text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.
